newsitem.title: UK: Defiant Princess Anne to return for Grand National.
newsitem.headline: Defiant Princess Anne to return for Grand National.

text.p: Police on Monday laid the tightest security net seen on a British racecourse for the running of the Grand National, being staged 48 hours after a suspected IRA bomb alert forced its abandonment.

Detectives warned racegoers to be extra-vigilant and said every one of them would be thoroughly searched on the way into the sprawling Aintree racecourse for the 150th running of the world's most famous steeplechase at 1600 GMT.
The Irish Republican Army has stepped up its campaign of violence against British rule in Northern Ireland in the run-up to Britain's May 1 election.

Two coded warnings were received just 30 minutes before Saturday's race at Aintree was due to start. Police mounted a huge security sweep, carrying out three controlled explosions on suspect packages but finding no bombs. Prime Minister John Major blamed the IRA for the race's cancellation.
Racecourse managers, overwhelmed by the support given to them by trainers, owners and the public, expect up to 10,000 people to come for Monday's free day out at the races.
"We are asking everyone to be extremely vigilant and report anything suspicious," a police spokesman said.
"There will be a high level of security in all areas and that will continue throughout the day," he said. Each racegoer will receive a leaflet with security tips.
Buckingham Palace confirmed that Princess Anne, Queen Elizabeth's horse-loving daughter, will return to the racecourse she had left so hurriedly on Saturday along with 70,000 other racegoers.
Thousands of race fans were stranded in nearby Liverpool overnight. A spokesman for the northwest England city proudly boasted that Liverpudlian hospitality was up to the challenge.

"It really has been the spirit of the wartime blitz," the spokesman said. Schools, churches and sports halls were hastily opened up and many families near the racecourse took pity on the stranded sports fans and offered food and accommodation.
Bookmakers looking forward to Britain's biggest gambling day of the year have pledged that all bets will stand for Monday's race.
Gamblers have already bet $120 million on the Grand National, which will now be contested over the awesome Aintree fences by 36 of the original 38 entries.
Jenny Pitman, who has trained two previous Grand National winners, was defiant. "We cannot be held to ransom by these people and neither can the country."
